idiom_name: Play session cookie (signed JWT) plus server-side CacheApi
implementation_notes: Play implements the session as a signed JWT cookie (PLAY_SESSION): request.session is the manager view, withSession writes it, withNewSession discards it, and maxAge sets both the cookie lifetime and the JWT exp claim. Because that payload is client-side and readable, the pattern's central store is realized separately with a named CacheApi (play.cache.bindCaches plus play-redis), keeping only an opaque identifier in the signed cookie. That combination - signed cookie for the identifier, cache for the state - is the idiomatic Scala realization; keep state out of the cookie itself.
code_sketch:
def login = Action { implicit request =>
  val user = authenticate(request)
  Redirect("/home").withSession("sid" -> sessionStore.create(user))  // signed cookie, id only
}
def logout = Action.async { implicit request =>
  sessionStore.invalidate(request.session.get("sid"))
  Future.successful(Redirect("/").withNewSession)                    // drop client cookie
}
pitfalls: The default Play session is client-side and only signed, not encrypted: any value placed there is visible to the user and replayable until maxAge.
The 4 KB cookie limit bounds the session; a real session store is a named cache, typically Redis.
Session changes are visible only to subsequent requests, so a modification without a redirect can read stale values in the same request.
Cache-based stores must tolerate eviction: entries are lost by design, so a session record must be reconstructible or backed by a database.
